content: A cell type refers to a specific morphological or functional form of a cell. When a cell transitions from one type to another, it undergoes a process known as cellular differentiation. In the three domains of life—Eukaryota, Bacteria, and Archaea—eukaryotes include organisms such as animals, humans, plants, algae, and protozoa. Prokaryotes, on the other hand, consist of bacteria and archaea, with archaea being a specialized group of prokaryotes. In animals, including humans, different cell types exhibit distinct responses to external stimuli. For example, the function of protein kinase A (PKA) varies depending on the specific cell type. Similarly, calcium also exerts cell type-specific actions in humans. This information is derived from Molecular Biology, Fourth Edition by Weaver, published as a McGraw-Hill International Edition.
